card.name: Llamerada
card.tagline: The rhythmic highland trot of Andean llama herders.
card.profile: The Llamerada is an Andean folk dance performed in Bolivia and Peru that mimically captures the pastoral life of highland llama herders and muleteers. Dancers advance in parallel male and female columns, spinning a woven sling (khorawa) while matching their footsteps to the light trotting pace of camelid caravans. Recognized as national cultural heritage in both Bolivia (2011) and Peru (2024), the dance blends economic history with ritual expressions of gratitude to Pachamama. Today, it forms a central visual element of major festivals such as the Carnaval de Oruro and the Festividad de la Virgen de la Candelaria.
card.insight: Founded in 1921, Oruro's Conjunto Tradicional Llamerada Zona Norte honours Andean llama herders with step-trots, woven slings, and vibrant headdresses.

card.profile_long:
Origins and History
The Llamerada represents the historical journey of camelid herders and muleteers who traveled from the high Andean altiplano to lower valleys to trade products, utilizing the llama as their primary pack animal. While certain researchers argue that the tradition holds ancient or Inca roots tied to pre-Hispanic Tahuantinsuyo and pastoral rituals, others locate its modern festive emergence in Bolivia's Oruro and Potosí regions. A major historical milestone includes the founding of the Conjunto Tradicional Llamerada Zona Norte in 1921 in Oruro. Historically documented in late 19th-century accounts of altiplano carnivals, the dance was officially designated as Cultural Heritage of Bolivia in 2011 and as National Cultural Heritage in Peru in 2024.

How It Is Danced
The choreography of the Llamerada is executed by male and female dancers positioned in two separate, parallel columns. Movements mimic the light, springy trotting motion of llamas traversing rugged mountain passes. Dancers execute synchronized forward and backward steps, interweaving choreographic formations while twirling a khorawa (a traditional woven sling) in their right hand to rhythmically simulate herding signals. A key figure known as the qañiachu—representing the dominant male llama—leads the group with disciplined, elegant figures, while some male dancers hold small sculpted llama figures in their left hand.

Music and Instruments
The dance is set to a rhythmic, continuous meter designed to match a light trotting gait. Traditional altiplano brass bands and native panpipe ensembles provide the melodic foundation, combining bright cadences with steady percussion beats. The tempo and musical arrangements have evolved over decades within urban fraternities while preserving the characteristic steady pacing that guides the synchronised spinning of the khorawa slings.

Costume and Setting
Dancers wear distinctive square cloth monteras (headdresses) trimmed with fringe, reminiscent of the traditional headwear of Aymara community leaders (Mama Talla). Footwear consists of abarcas or ojotas. Men wear wool or silk shirts, knee-length bayeta trousers, colorful woven sashes (chumpi), cayto socks, and a brightly pattern aguayo shawl wrapped across the chest paired with a coiled rope. Female dancers wear multiple layered polleras (petticoats), an aguayo draped across the torso, and a blouse. Some male performers carry plaster masks depicting puckered lips to symbolize whistling to the herd.

Occasions and Meaning
Beyond its representation of herding and trade caravans, the Llamerada maintains historical ritual significance linked to Pachamama (Mother Earth) and livestock fertility. It is performed in major religious and civic celebrations across the Andes, including the Carnaval de Oruro, the Fiesta del Gran Poder, the Festividad de Urkupiña, and the Festividad de la Virgen de la Candelaria in Puno. Through these performances, urban and mestizo communities reaffirm their cultural identity and ancestral connection to the highland environment.

sections.notable_figures: The 'Conjunto Tradicional Llamerada Zona Norte', founded in 1921 in Oruro, is documented as the oldest formal ensemble dedicated to this dance. Lead figures within fraternities include the qañiachu, who guides the troupe's movements, and the tatalas, community figures of higher hierarchy traditionally wearing black attire.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is actively performed across both Bolivia (notably in Oruro, La Paz, and Potosí) and Peru (specifically in the Puno region). In Peru, it is celebrated as the 'Llamerada puneña', forming an integral part of the Festividad de la Virgen de la Candelaria. Related but distinct regional herding dances include Karwani in La Paz, Llama Llama in Oruro, and Llameritos de Orcopampa in Peru.
sections.lineage: Rooted in pre-Hispanic Aymara and Quechua pastoral traditions, the Llamerada evolved from altiplano camelid herding routines into organized festival performance arts across southern Peru and western Bolivia.

claims.text: Llamerada represents the llama herders who traveled between the altiplano and the valleys.
Male dancers traditionally hold a little llama in their left hand while spinning a sling in their right.
The dance was declared Cultural Heritage of Bolivia by Law 136 in 2011.
Peru recognized the Llamerada Puneña as National Cultural Heritage in January 2024.
The Conjunto Tradicional Llamerada Zona Norte was founded in 1921.
Dancers move in two separate lines, one of men and one of women.
